logline: A battle-hardened teenage soldier with no concept of civilian life is assigned to protect a high school girl who holds secrets she doesn't know she has - and has to navigate mecha combat and high school comedy simultaneously.

renewal.note: The franchise ran across four seasons (2002-2018) and is considered complete following Invisible Victory, which adapts the final light novel arcs. No further continuation has been announced.

bollymeter.basis: ANN weighted mean of 7.996 (Very good) from 7,293 ratings. Critics praised the mecha detail and the central chemistry but found the genre-blending uneven - the show is better when it picks one register.

pull_quotes.text: FMP throws mecha, tsundere heroine, and high-octane action into the mix - resulting in a tense series lightened by high school comedy.

seasons.review_body: Full Metal Panic! launched on WOWOW in January 2002, with Gonzo adapting Shoji Gatoh's light novel series about Sousuke Sagara - a soldier from a private anti-terrorist organisation who has no frame of reference for civilian life and is deployed undercover in a Tokyo high school to protect Kaname Chidori. The premise's tension between military mecha action and high-school-comedy register was the franchise's defining feature and its main critical dividing line. ANN's weighted mean of 7.996 from 7,293 ratings (ranked #17 on the platform at that time) placed it firmly in the 'very good' tier. Reviews that found it worked praised Gonzo's meticulous Arm Slave (mecha) design and the natural antagonism between Sousuke's literal-minded military logic and Kaname's exasperated civilian perspective. Reviews that found it uneven noted that the tonal shift between action episodes and comedy episodes never fully resolved into a single coherent identity. The relationship between Sousuke and Kaname - at once a bodyguard premise and a slow-burn romance - is the series' main draw and what generates its most consistently praised moments.

episode_reviews.title: The Guy I Kinda Like is a Sergeant
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The franchise sets up both its action credentials and its comedic register in the first episode - Sousuke's tactical paranoia applied to mundane high school situations is the joke the series will run for 24 episodes, and it lands well initially.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Sousuke defusing what he believes is a bomb on school grounds - the central character dynamic established in pure comedy form.

bollymeter.basis: Fumoffu is the most purely comedic entry in the franchise and the one most critics consider the most consistent - Kyoto Animation's comic timing elevated the material. ANN reviewers noted it as the franchise's best tonal execution.

seasons.review_body: Full Metal Panic? Fumoffu was Kyoto Animation's first major franchise production and 12 episodes of deliberately mecha-free high-school comedy. Kyoto Animation's reputation for fluid character animation and precise comedic timing - later to become genre-defining on Lucky Star and K-On! - was already visible in Fumoffu's timing and expressions. The tonal consistency that Season 1 lacked is Fumoffu's main virtue; by committing fully to comedy rather than genre-blending, the shorter run lands with fewer rough edges. The Bonta-kun mascot costume arc is the franchise's most quoted comic material. Fumoffu works as a standalone entry for viewers with no interest in the mecha action - it is effectively a pure-comedy spinoff - and as palate-cleansing relief between the heavier military storylines. Kyoto Animation returned for The Second Raid the following year.
seasons.season_over_season: Fumoffu strips out the mecha action entirely and runs a pure comedy season - shorter, funnier, and more consistent than Season 1's tonal oscillation.

bollymeter.basis: The Second Raid is widely regarded as the franchise's dramatic peak - Kyoto Animation pushed character development beyond the comedy-action balance into genuinely dark psychological territory. ANN's Theron Martin called it the entry that pushed character developments beyond what the original achieved.

seasons.review_body: The Second Raid, the franchise's second Kyoto Animation season, aired July 2005 across 13 episodes and represents the point at which Full Metal Panic! stopped being a genre-blend entertainment and became something darker. Kyoto Animation pushed Sousuke's psychological unravelling - his identity crisis when separated from his mission and from Kaname - into genuinely affecting territory. The tonal pivot away from high-school comedy is near-total; the dramatic and psychological registers carry the entire season. The 13-episode run is tightly paced and the mecha sequences benefit from Kyoto Animation's animation quality at its pre-K-On peak. The Second Raid is the franchise entry that most rewards investment in the character arcs since Season 1 and the one most likely to convert those who found the original tonally inconsistent.
seasons.season_over_season: The Second Raid ditches comedy almost entirely in favour of psychological depth - a darker, tighter season that critics consider the franchise peak.

bollymeter.basis: Invisible Victory - produced by Xebec after a 13-year gap - adapts the final light novel arcs faithfully but divided critics: some praised the return to the darker register of The Second Raid; others noted the production values as a step down from Kyoto Animation's benchmark.

seasons.review_body: Invisible Victory returned the franchise to screens in April 2018 after a 13-year hiatus, with Xebec replacing Kyoto Animation as producer. The franchise gap was unusual and meant the fanbase returned with strong expectations. Xebec's adaptation of the final light novel arcs is faithful to the source material and tonally aligned with The Second Raid's darker register. The production values are the main point of divergence from earlier seasons - the animation is serviceable but lacks the fluidity that Kyoto Animation had established as the franchise's visual benchmark. The 12-episode run adapts a dense stretch of source material and the pacing is noticeably compressed in places. As a franchise finale it provides sufficient closure for long-term fans; as an entry point it is inaccessible without the prior seasons. Invisible Victory earns its place as a completion rather than a fresh creative statement.
seasons.season_over_season: Invisible Victory closes the franchise after 13 years away - faithful to the source novels and tonally aligned with The Second Raid, but Xebec's production can't match Kyoto Animation's visual benchmark.
